title: Saka Nankana day
hookLine: each February Sikhs remember the martyrs of Nankana, 1921

lines: NOT A BIRTHDAY, NOT A FAIR.
cards: Not every day on the Sikh calendar is a birthday or a harvest fair. Some are kept for grief. One of them belongs to Nankana Sahib, the town tradition holds as Guru Nanak's birthplace.
On a morning in the last century, reformers came to its gurdwara to pray, and were killed there without lifting a hand. This path has already walked through that morning.
Sikhs still keep it on the calendar, and today's practice asks for something small: one lamp.

teach.b: This begins a new stretch of the path: the calendar of memory. How a people keeps grief says a lot about them.
Sikhs call a remembered episode of martyrdom like this a saka.
Saka Nankana is that morning, and it remembers the reformers who walked into the gurdwara at Nankana Sahib, sat before the Guru Granth Sahib, and were attacked inside. These were not soldiers.

Accounts say they had pledged not to strike back, and they kept the pledge. So the day doesn't remember a battle. It remembers a refusal: to answer violence with violence, even at the cost of their lives.

It's kept with kirtan, and with the Ardas, the standing prayer that closes Sikh gatherings, which remembers those who gave their lives in service of the gurdwaras. Pilgrims gather at Nankana Sahib itself.
The Mool Mantar, the opening of the Guru Granth Sahib on Ang 1, names the One as nirbhau and nirvair: without fear, without enmity.
In the telling Sikhs keep, the reformers walked in without fear, and did not answer with enmity. So the day isn't kept with speeches against anyone. It's kept with a hymn and a prayer.

how: On the yearly remembrance of Saka Nankana Sahib, gurdwaras hold kirtan and the Ardas in memory of the reformers, and pilgrims gather at Nankana Sahib.

games.q: it's the remembrance of Saka Nankana at your gurdwara. what sits at the center of the day?
o: kirtan and the Ardas before the Guru Granth Sahib.
games.why: kirtan and the Ardas, before the Guru Granth Sahib. the reformers did not answer with enmity, and the day is kept the same way.

practice: If you have a candle or small lamp and it's safe, light it and set it where you can see it; if not, rest your eyes on any small light near you, a screen dimmed low, a window.

Let the flame stand for people who came to pray and did not strike back, and breathe slowly with two words to rest on: without fear, without enmity. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out.
